identity.title: Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing the Training Origins of Interpretable LLM Units

problem.claim: The paper addresses tracing interpretable LLM units to their causal origins in training data.

gap.claim: Existing mechanistic-interpretability work had identified interpretable circuits, but their causal training-data origins remained elusive.

contributions.claim: Introduces mechanistic data attribution (MDA), a scalable influence-function framework for tracing interpretable units to specific training samples.
Reports that repetitive structural data, such as LaTeX and XML, acts as a mechanistic catalyst, and links induction-head interventions with changes in ICL capability.
Proposes a mechanistic data-augmentation pipeline intended to accelerate circuit convergence across model scales and steer LLM developmental trajectories.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present MDA as a scalable framework for mechanistically attributing interpretable units to training samples, alongside a mechanistic augmentation pipeline.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report on the Pythia family that removing or augmenting a small fraction of high-influence samples significantly modulates interpretable-head emergence, while random interventions show no effect.
The authors report that interventions targeting induction-head formation concurrently change ICL capability.
The authors report that mechanistic data augmentation consistently accelerates circuit convergence across model scales.

narrative_sequence.summary: Interpretable circuits are known, but their causal origins in training data are unresolved.
MDA uses influence functions to trace interpretable units to specific training samples.
On Pythia models, targeted high-influence-sample interventions modulate interpretable-head emergence, unlike random interventions; repetitive structural data is identified as a catalyst.
Induction-head interventions are reported to alter ICL capability, supporting the proposed induction-head–ICL link.
A mechanistic augmentation pipeline is proposed to accelerate circuit convergence across scales.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects attribution to targeted data interventions, then reports distinct outcomes for high-influence versus random samples.

lessons.interpretation: Pairing an explanatory attribution method with selective intervention can make a mechanistic claim more testable than attribution alone.
lessons.application: For a paper claiming data origins of a learned behavior, rank candidate samples, intervene on a small targeted subset, and include a matched random-intervention comparison.
lessons.exception: This design may be unsuitable when influence estimates are unavailable, interventions cannot be isolated, or the behavior lacks a measurable developmental outcome.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the intervention fractions, influence-function implementation, outcome metrics, model checkpoints, or statistical details.
The reported causal effects and convergence acceleration are not independently verified here; conditions and magnitude of the ICL change are unspecified.
The abstract does not establish how the proposed pipeline compares with other data-augmentation or training-steering methods.
